statement: Assume fatigued threshold speed is lower than the fresh value after prolonged running: about 5.5% lower after 90 min at or below threshold, with large individual spread; use population prior until at least 3 comparable athlete runs exist, then personalise.
unit: % decline of lactate-threshold speed after 90 min
appliesTo: recreational to well-trained runners targeting half marathon or longer; lab-derived, running

statement: For prolonged heavy-intensity work around 2 h, a larger default decline of about 10% in critical speed/threshold is plausible (range under 1% to about 32%); this is cycling-derived and unvalidated for running, so use only as an upper-bound sensitivity for marathon-pace planning, not as the default.
unit: % decline in critical power/speed after 2 h heavy intensity
appliesTo: marathon and longer plans, heavy-intensity efforts of 2 h or more

statement: Expect HR at constant easy pace to rise about 5.5% over 90 min in temperate lab conditions; treat drift near this value as normal and not as evidence of lost fitness. Do not apply this number to hot, dehydrated or ultra-duration runs.
unit: % rise in HR over 90 min at constant easy pace
appliesTo: recreational runners, temperate conditions, easy runs of about 90 min

statement: For marathon-distance efforts with HR and speed, compute decoupling as the ratio of (%HRmax divided by speed as %CS) in the 35-40 km segment to the same in the 5-10 km segment; flag onset when it exceeds 1.025; band low <1.1, moderate 1.1 to <1.2, high >=1.2 for feedback only.
appliesTo: marathon races with HR and speed data; needs grade-adjusted pace and temperature/hydration tagging before comparing runs

statement: For long runs shorter or longer than a marathon, compute a proportionally scaled decoupling (late segment vs early reference segment of the same fractional position, e.g. 5-10 km vs 35-40 km of 42.2 km) and label it a low-confidence proxy; do not apply the Smyth bands as fitness grades.
value: early reference at ~12-24% of distance, late at ~83-95% of distance
appliesTo: long runs of 60 min to 3 h; engineering extension of a marathon-specific method

statement: Do not change race-pace targets or fitness estimates from a single run's drift or decoupling; require several comparable runs and use pace-adjusted cardiac cost rather than raw HR; attribute late slowing to pacing before attributing drift to durability.
appliesTo: all runners; engine fitness and pacing updates

statement: Treat two long runs as comparable only if duration, relative intensity, temperature and fuelling/fluid status are similar; exclude or tag non-comparable runs from the durability estimate. Numeric tolerances are conservative engineering defaults, not literature values.
value: duration within 20%; ambient temperature within 5 C; same fuelling/fluid flag
appliesTo: free-living run data used to estimate durability

statement: In hot conditions HR rises with falling capacity (HR +17-19% and VO2max loss within 45 min at 35 C), so do not hold a fixed HR zone; prescribe by pace/RPE with a temperature adjustment, and do not compare drift to temperate runs. The temperature at which to switch and the size of the correction are not established; default to flagging runs at or above 25 C.
appliesTo: all runners; runs in warm or hot conditions

statement: Drift and VO2peak loss grow with dehydration, so require a hydration status input (fluid taken or estimated body-mass loss) for hot long runs; flag runs with no fluid or estimated body-mass loss above about 2% and exclude them from durability estimation. The 2% cut-off is a conservative reading of cycling data (0.7% loss with fluid showed little VO2peak loss; 3.7% without fluid showed about 9%).
appliesTo: runs longer than 90 min in warm conditions; evidence from cycling in 30-33 C

statement: For half-marathon and longer goals, include a long run of at least 90 min every 7 to 14 days once training status allows, because regular long runs and higher volume are associated with smaller economy decay; the evidence is associative.
appliesTo: runners targeting half marathon or longer with adequate base; evidence from well-trained men

statement: In marathon-and-longer builds, optionally finish selected long runs with race-pace or progressive-intensity work; conservative default of the final 20% of duration at goal marathon pace, at most once every 2 weeks, never in heat-flagged or low-fluid conditions. Proposed in a narrative review, untested.
value: final 20% of long-run duration at marathon pace, at most once per 2 weeks
appliesTo: runners in marathon or longer builds with a consistent long-run base

statement: For well-trained runners targeting long races, include two weekly sessions of maximal strength plus plyometrics for at least 10 weeks ahead of the specific build; an RCT showed better economy durability and fatigued high-intensity performance. For women, novices and older runners the effect is untested, so use as a moderate-confidence extrapolation and progress conservatively.
appliesTo: well-trained runners (RCT in men); extrapolation to others

statement: Use a sex term in durability and decoupling priors, but keep it weak (males larger and earlier decoupling: 1.17 vs 1.12 ratio, onset 25.0 vs 26.3 km) and let athlete data override it after a few comparable runs; no sex-specific fuelling change is justified.
appliesTo: marathon-distance decoupling priors and durability descriptor initialisation

statement: When a prior marathon with HR and speed exists, add decoupling magnitude and onset (or lab threshold decline) as optional predictors in the marathon time model; population-level error reduction was 6.45% to 5.16%. Validate against the athlete's own results before letting it change pacing targets.
value: decoupling magnitude + onset (or % threshold decline after 90 min)
appliesTo: marathon prediction for runners with a prior marathon with HR and speed data

statement: Do not extrapolate 1-3 h drift or threshold-decline priors to 100-mile or other ultra efforts, and do not infer fitness from HR drift in sessions beyond about 3 to 4 h; drift reverses and changes character over 12-50 h. Steer ultra long efforts by pace, RPE, fuelling and terrain, and use drift only descriptively. DFA-a1 and respiratory frequency are optional, device-dependent extras.
appliesTo: ultramarathon and 100-mile plans, sessions over 3 h
